title: Finding Planets by Their Shadows
subtitle: Measure a transit, weigh what it tells you, and find what is hiding
body:
Step 1 of 30 read

A planet you cannot see

How can you find a planet you cannot see, and measure how big it is? You will watch a star dim as its planet crosses in front of it, predict how deep the dip will be, then read the depth off the light curve and turn it into a size.

On screen is HD 209458, a slightly hotter and more massive relative of the Sun about 160 light years away in Pegasus, with a planet on a three and a half day orbit. The view is zoomed far in to show the pair. Sizes on screen are not to scale: the planet is drawn smaller against its star than it really is, as every planet is, while the light curve works from the real sizes (details under Sizes).

💡 Everything in this investigation is measurable from what is on screen. Clicking selects an object without opening the inspector card, and placing new objects is switched off so a stray click cannot alter the system you are measuring.

title: Finding Planets by Their Shadows
subtitle: Measure a transit, weigh what it tells you, and find what is hiding
body:
Step 7 of 30 question

From a depth to a size

Suppose a survey reports a clean, repeating 1% dip: δ = 0.0100.

What is Rp / R★ for a 1% dip?

That matches. The square root of 0.01 is 0.1: the planet is a tenth of the star’s radius. Around a Sun-like star that is roughly Jupiter-sized, which is exactly why every transiting planet found before about 2005 was a hot Jupiter. They were the only ones anybody could see. To check a result like this, square it and see that the depth comes back.

title: Finding Planets by Their Shadows
subtitle: Measure a transit, weigh what it tells you, and find what is hiding
body:
Step 30 of 30 read

What you did, and where it goes next

Every radius you found is a ratio to the star, made better three times over, and each correction rested on something besides the dip: how the star's edge darkens, how the orbit is tilted to us, what else shines in the same aperture. A planet's radius is only as good as those.

TESS, JWST and PLATO are measuring transits now, and behind every one of their planets is the follow-up of the last three steps: somebody has to look at the host star with a big enough telescope to find out what else is there.

💡 A note on numbers: the survey results quoted here come from the Robo-AO Kepler Survey and the SOAR TESS Survey, both of which set out to image every planet-candidate host they could reach. The Robo-AO census covers 3,857 Kepler hosts; the SOAR program has observed close to 3,000 TESS targets and finds a median primary-host radius correction of about 1.07, rising to 1.33 for the worst tenth.
